stimulus.title: Humanities: What Is an Old Building?
stimulus.text:
In the middle of the nineteenth century, many of Europe's great medieval churches were in poor condition. Centuries of weather, war, neglect, and well-meaning alteration had left them cracked, patched, and in some cases half-ruined. Some had been stripped of their sculpture during revolutions; others had been modernized in styles that clashed with their original design. Out of the effort to save them came one of the most enduring arguments in the history of architecture, an argument not about how to repair old buildings, exactly, but about what it means for an old building to be authentic.

On one side stood the French architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc, who oversaw the restoration of a number of France's most famous medieval buildings. Viollet-le-Duc was a brilliant scholar of Gothic construction, and his ambition was correspondingly large. To restore a building, he wrote, is not to maintain it or repair it but to reestablish it in a finished state that may never have existed at any given moment. Where a church had been left incomplete, or altered by later builders, he was willing to design and build what he believed its original makers would have built, had they been able.

On the other side stood the English critic John Ruskin, for whom this approach was not merely mistaken but destructive. Restoration, Ruskin argued, was “the most total destruction which a building can suffer,” because it replaced the actual marks of the original builders, including their particular chisel strokes, their irregularities, and the wear of centuries, with a modern imitation. The value of an old building lay precisely in its age and in the labor of the specific people who made it. A restored church might look more complete, but it would be, in his view, a kind of lie. Better to protect a building with careful maintenance, Ruskin urged, and when it could no longer stand, to let it fall.

It is tempting to cast this disagreement as a contest between boldness and caution, or between imagination and respect. But both men loved medieval architecture deeply, and both believed they were honoring it. Their difference lay in where they located a building's value. For Viollet-le-Duc, value resided in the design, the idea of the building, which a skilled architect could understand and complete. For Ruskin, value resided in the physical object itself, in the irreplaceable material history that no design could reproduce.

The practical consequences of these views can still be seen. Some buildings restored in the nineteenth century carry towers, spires, and ornaments that are, in effect, Victorian-era additions dressed in medieval style. Many visitors cannot tell the difference, and some of these additions have become beloved in their own right; several cities have had to decide whether a celebrated nineteenth-century addition is now old enough to deserve protection itself. Meanwhile, the movement Ruskin helped inspire, which favored repair over reinvention, shaped the conservation principles adopted in the following century, many of which call for new work to be clearly distinguishable from old.

Yet neither position escapes difficulty when applied strictly. Ruskin's approach, followed to its logical end, would allow much of the world's architectural heritage to crumble rather than be touched. Viollet-le-Duc's approach, followed to its logical end, would allow a confident architect to replace history with his own theory of it. Even the decision to do nothing is a decision, with consequences that someone must answer for. Most conservators today work somewhere between these poles, making case-by-case judgments about when a missing element should be rebuilt and when an absence should simply be respected.

The debate endures because the question at its center has no final answer. When we stand in front of an old building, are we looking at an idea that happens to be made of stone, or at stone that happens to carry an idea? Each generation of architects answers a little differently, and each answer leaves its own marks, which future generations, in turn, will have to decide whether to keep.

Where a church had been left incomplete, or altered by later builders, he was willing to design and build what he believed its original makers would have built, had they been able.

On the other side stood the English critic John Ruskin, for whom this approach was not merely mistaken but destructive. Restoration, Ruskin argued, was “the most total destruction which a building can suffer,” because it replaced the actual marks of the original builders, including their particular chisel strokes, their irregularities, and the wear of centuries, with a modern imitation. The value of an old building lay precisely in its age and in the labor of the specific people who made it. A restored church might look more complete, but it would be, in his view, a kind of lie. Better to protect a building with careful maintenance, Ruskin urged, and when it could no longer stand, to let it fall.

It is tempting to cast this disagreement as a contest between boldness and caution, or between imagination and respect. But both men loved medieval architecture deeply, and both believed they were honoring it. Their difference lay in where they located a building's value. For Viollet-le-Duc, value resided in the design, the idea of the building, which a skilled architect could understand and complete. For Ruskin, value resided in the physical object itself, in the irreplaceable material history that no design could reproduce.

The practical consequences of these views can still be seen. Some buildings restored in the nineteenth century carry towers, spires, and ornaments that are, in effect, Victorian-era additions dressed in medieval style. Many visitors cannot tell the difference, and some of these additions have become beloved in their own right; several cities have had to decide whether a celebrated nineteenth-century addition is now old enough to deserve protection itself. Meanwhile, the movement Ruskin helped inspire, which favored repair over reinvention, shaped the conservation principles adopted in the following century, many of which call for new work to be clearly distinguishable from old.

Yet neither position escapes difficulty when applied strictly. Ruskin's approach, followed to its logical end, would allow much of the world's architectural heritage to crumble rather than be touched. Viollet-le-Duc's approach, followed to its logical end, would allow a confident architect to replace history with his own theory of it. Even the decision to do nothing is a decision, with consequences that someone must answer for. Most conservators today work somewhere between these poles, making case-by-case judgments about when a missing element should be rebuilt and when an absence should simply be respected.

The debate endures because the question at its center has no final answer. When we stand in front of an old building, are we looking at an idea that happens to be made of stone, or at stone that happens to carry an idea? Each generation of architects answers a little differently, and each answer leaves its own marks, which future generations, in turn, will have to decide whether to keep.
